characters: Georgina: a 14-year-old girl with a campaign poster and a notebook of student complaints.
Sedem: a 14-year-old boy, her rival, with a bag of sweets and a loud, friendly voice.
Mr Gbeku: the school’s electoral officer, a teacher with a ballot box and a voters’ register.
The assembly ground: a school ground with posters, a ballot box and a long queue of students.

narrationPlan.voice: Lively campaign voices; a calm, impartial voice for Mr Gbeku the electoral officer
narrationPlan.pace: Campaign-bright and persuasive, steady in the speeches (about 120 words per minute)
notes: Read dialogue with a different voice for each character.
Pause for two seconds at each question activity.
Never rush the last page: let the ending land.

music: Upbeat campaign highlife with a rally drum; a thoughtful, steady tune at the result (placeholder)
culturalNotes: The school, candidates and officers are invented. Many Ghanaian schools elect a Students’ Representative Council (SRC) and prefects; details differ.
The story does not name any real party or politician. Sedem’s sweets are shown as a lesson, not as a comment on real elections.
The letter on page 7 is formal, with “Dear Madam” and “Yours faithfully”, to show the difference from informal letters.
reviewQuestions: Is the language right for the stated age band and reading level?
Is anything here inaccurate, stereotyped or unsafe for children?
Check the SRC rules and roles with the school’s SRC patron or head teacher.
Check that the story does not suggest that sweets or gifts are always bribes; discuss how to run a fair campaign.
Check the formal letter layout (addresses, date, subject line, “Yours faithfully”) against the BECE marking scheme.

teacherGuide.overview: A story about fair campaigning, honest promises and the real work of a student leader. It also contrasts a formal letter with the informal letters in earlier stories.
learningGoals: Explain the difference between an honest promise and an empty one.
Contrast a formal letter with an informal one.
beforeReading: Ask: what makes a good leader? A good promise?
whileReading: At page 3, ask learners which promise they trust, and why.
afterReading: Run a mock class election with a secret ballot and public count.
Write a formal letter to the head teacher requesting permission for an event.
discussion: Why does a secret ballot matter?
Is it ever right to make a promise you are not sure you can keep?
reflection: What is one thing you would do for your school if you were elected?

mathsExtension.task: Georgina wins by 42 votes. Sedem gets 118 votes. How many does Georgina get?
How many votes in total, and what percentage did Georgina win?

support: Give learners a formal letter frame with boxes: sender’s address, date, receiver, Dear…, reason, request, Yours faithfully.
stretch: Write a campaign speech with three promises that the SRC can actually keep.

culturalNotes: The school, candidates and officers are invented. Many Ghanaian schools elect a Students’ Representative Council (SRC) and prefects; details differ.
The story does not name any real party or politician. Sedem’s sweets are shown as a lesson, not as a comment on real elections.
The letter on page 7 is formal, with “Dear Madam” and “Yours faithfully”, to show the difference from informal letters.
localiseThis: Use your school’s real SRC rules. Do not use real party names; keep the exercise school-based.

factCheck.claim: A formal letter has the writer’s address, the date, the recipient’s designation and full address, “Dear Sir/Madam”, a title or heading, “Yours faithfully/Yours sincerely”, the writer’s signature and full name; the language must be polite, clear and persuasive with no contractions, slang or colloquialism.
